senses: One who advocates for brinkmanship.
ety: Back-formation from brinkmanship, equivlent to brink + -man.
examples: It compels the 'brinkmen' to realise that, if they seek to make war on the Soviet Union, they cannot count on cooperation from Britain or France, and probably not from Western Germany.

The brinkmen Kennan abhorred were supreme realists, and if "the assumption that state behavior is a fit subject for moral judgment" is baseless, then anything, even the realism of atomic blackmail, would be permissible.

The Syrian force was pulled back quickly and with reportedly heavy losses, but it stayed around long enough to remind the world that the Syrians are still the biggest blusterers and brinkmen in the Middle East.

senses: Having a distinctive odor.
ety: From Middle English odorous, from Medieval Latin odōrōsus, equivalent to odor + -ous.
examples: The table was piled with odorous lilies.

senses: A person who makes maps.
ety: From map + maker.

senses: A tiny piece of bread, either one that falls from bread as it is cut or eaten, or one made deliberately by crumbling bread.
One in a series of clues leading to a person or place.
ety: From bread + crumb. The computing and figurative senses allude to the German fairy tale Hansel and Gretel, where Hansel leaves a trail of breadcrumbs to find the way back home when venturing into the woods.

senses: Having ridges.
ety: From Middle English rigged, riggid, ryggyd, rugged, equivalent to ridge + -ed.

senses: A profitable thing or scheme.
ety: Deliberate misspelling of stock, possibly under the influence of stink in reference to stocks relating to amateur or bad decisions, or financial loss. Compare stronk (“strong”), thonk (“think”).

senses: A mock title.
ety: From elegance + -y or elegant + -cy.

senses: Very dry, lacking humidity and water.
Adapted to live in a very dry habitat.
ety: From Ancient Greek ξηρός (xērós, “dry”) + English -ic.

senses: A traditional formal way of sitting in Japan, by kneeling with the legs folded underneath the thighs and the buttocks resting on the heels, with ankles turned outward.
ety: From Japanese 正座 (seiza, literally “proper sitting”).
examples: She arranged herself with her legs folded beneath her, spine erect, echoing “seiza”, the Japanese sitting position adopted in formal situations.

senses: The property or degree of being allergenic.
ety: From allergenic + -ity.

senses: Containing calories.
Synonym of calorific (“high in calories and thus likely fattening”).
Synonym of calorific (“relating to or producing heat or other energy”).
ety: From calorie + -ic. From French calorique, coined by French chemist Antoine Lavoisier, from Latin calor (“heat”).

senses: The precipitation of ash from a volcanic eruption.
ety: From ash + fall.

senses: An internal courtyard, surrounded by walls but open to the sky
ety: Borrowed from Italian.

senses: In favor of the abolition of any particular institution or practice.
In favor of the abolition of slavery.
ety: First attested in 1788. abolition + -ist.

senses: Susceptible to influence by suggestion; easily swayed.
ety: From suggest + -ible.

senses: A pattern of interconnected objects.
The tripe made from the second compartment of the stomach of a cow (or other ruminant).
ety: Borrowed from Latin rēticulum (“net”). Doublet of reticle, reticule, and Reticulum.

senses: An Ancient Greek circular dance accompanied by a chorus.
ety: From Ancient Greek χορεία (khoreía).

senses: The quality of being artificial or produced unnaturally.
Something artificial.
ety: From artificial + -ity.

senses: A large machine used to recover bulk material from a stockpile.
ety: From reclaim + -er.

senses: A toasted grain or grains of corn, a traditional snack in Peru.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish cancha, borrowed from Quechua kamcha.

senses: Unlimited power; commonly attributed to a deity or deities.
ety: From Late Middle English omnipotens, from Old French omnipotence, from Latin omnipotentia.

senses: A sweet fortified wine made in Madeira, originally from the malvasia grape.
ety: Via Middle English malmesye from Middle Dutch malemeseye, from Italian via Old French, ultimately from Ancient Greek Μονεμβασία (Monembasía, “Monemvasia”, a city on the Peloponnese), from μόνος (mónos, “only one”) + ἔμβασις (émbasis, “entering into”, ἐν- + βάσις). Doublet of malvoisie.

senses: A former unit of volumic radioactivity: the quantity of radon (ignoring its daughters) per litre of air which ionizes a sustained current of 0.001 esu.
ety: From German Mache, surname of Heinrich Mache.

senses: A type of landslide characterized by large flows of mud and water.
The dried-out product of such a flow.
ety: From mud + flow.
examples: Some believe an earthquake set off the disaster, others that the mudflow was caused by a company drilling for natural gas.

senses: To form a synapse.
To undergo synapsis.
ety: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek σύναψις (súnapsis, “conjunction”), from συνάπτω (sunáptō, “to clasp”). Introduced by neurophysiologist Charles Scott Sherrington.

senses: The act of reupholstering furniture
ety: From re- + upholstery.
examples: Sofas and chairs can be coordinated into any design through reupholstery or slipcovers. Reupholstery requires a fabric selection appropriate for your piece.

senses: A long sheepskin coat made of thick wool, worn by Tibetans.
ety: Borrowed from Tibetan ཕྱུ་པ (phyu pa), from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba). Doublet of jupe and jubbah.
examples: DRESSED in a pale blue, floor-length chuba, Paige Wilson silently mouthed a paragraph-long greeting, in Tibetan, that she was about to deliver to the Dalai Lama.

senses: A style of Afro-Caribbean music that originated in Trinidad and Tobago during the early to the mid-19th century and spread to the rest of the Caribbean Antilles and Venezuela by the mid-20th century.
A song in this style of music.
ety: Originally Trinidad English, an alteration of kaiso, perhaps ultimately of African origin; Allsopp 1996 suggests Ibibio ka iso (“come on”), used to urge dancers on. The spelling reflects a later folk-etymological assimilation with the mythological name Calypso.

senses: An Aramaic translation of the Tanakh written or compiled between the Second Temple period and the early Middle Ages.
ety: From Hebrew תַּרְגּוּם (targúm, “translation”).

senses: To treat with tenderness.
ety: From en- + tender. Doublet of intenerate.

senses: The reintroduction of minerals to the soil for agricultural benefit.
ety: From re- + mineralization.

senses: To fix again.
ety: From re- + fix.

senses: Honour, pride; reputation.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani عِزَّت ('izzat) / इज़्ज़त (izzat), from Classical Persian عِزَّت (izzat), from Arabic عِزَّة (ʕizza).

senses: Pointed; ending in a point or points.
ety: From Latin punctum (“point”). See point and punctuate.

senses: A type of instrumental composition based on multipart vocal settings of canzoni, produced chiefly in the 16th and 17th centuries
ety: Borrowed from Italian canzona.
examples: Mr. Milnes had a turn in the spotlight with a canzona for solo organ by Johann Caspar Kerll.

senses: A grid of geosynthetic material used to reinforce soil and other materials.
ety: From geo- + grid.

senses: Covered with bristles.
Easily antagonized; irascible; prone to bristling.
ety: From Middle English bristli, brustly, equivalent to bristle + -y.

senses: Someone who receives a gift from a donor.
ety: From donor + -ee (attested since 1523).
examples: John became the donee of the bone marrow donated by his brother.
But this donee or this purchasoure shall take to their profyte all the vesture standyng vpon or beyng with in the sayd groūde

senses: Acne on the back.
ety: Blend of back + acne. Equivalent to back + -ne.

senses: A kind of Romanian folk song, often of lament, which has also been adopted into klezmer (Ashkenazi Jewish) music.
ety: Borrowed from Romanian doină.
examples: For quotations using this term, see Citations:doina.
